title: Rotating an array
questions: How do three in-place reversals rotate [A,B,C,D,E] right by 2 while restoring order within each moved group? What happens to the same elements during the three phases?

slide.title: Three reversals rotate the same array
slide.narrative:
The full reversal moves the last group to the front, but reverses the order inside both groups. The two partial reversals restore each group's order without changing its new position.

All three phases change the same array. An empty array returns unchanged. For a nonempty array, normalization maps an integer count to the range from zero through `items.length - 1`.

fileSummaries.summary: Three in-place reversals replace repeated pop/unshift operations for right rotation.

svgIllustration.title: Group positions change; group order is restored
svgIllustration.takeaway: The full reversal exchanges the groups. Each partial reversal restores order inside one group.
svgIllustration.assumptions: The example uses [A,B,C,D,E] and integer k = 2. Rows show successive states of the same array, not separate arrays.

plan.question: How do the same elements move through three reversals while order inside both groups is restored?
plan.visualApproach: Show four aligned array states. Keep positions in fixed columns and give each original group a distinct shape. Label each reversal with its inclusive range.
plan.whyThisForm: Aligned states show group position and internal order together. The reader can compare all phases without remembering an earlier frame.
plan.encodings: Columns represent array indices. Squares identify the original ABC group; circles identify the original DE group. Outlines below each changed row mark the reversed range. Shape and element labels preserve group identity without color.

frames.title: Both moved groups recover their original order
frames.caption: Read downward. The marked range is reversed to produce that row. Each range includes both endpoints.
